subject: Cognitive Science
title: Prosocial Behavior in Toddlers
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Prosocial Behavior in Toddlers.

hook.text: A fourteen-month-old sees an adult drop a clothespin. Without being asked, the toddler hands it back.

buildup.text: Felix Warneken showed that toddlers help spontaneously—opening doors, picking up dropped items.

discovery.text: This helping behavior appears across cultures and before any moral teaching from parents.

twist.text: Rewarding children for helping actually reduces future helping. Rewards undermine natural motives.

climax.text: Human helpfulness may be an evolved trait—chimpanzees also help, but far less consistently.

punchline.text: Kindness comes before anyone teaches it.

quiz.question: What happens when children are rewarded for helping?
options: They help less in the future

details.summary: Toddlers as young as 14 months spontaneously help others, sharing objects and assisting with tasks without being taught or rewarded. This early prosocial behavior suggests that helping is a natural human tendency that emerges before cultural instruction fully takes effect.
details.whyItMatters: Early prosociality challenges the view that humans are fundamentally selfish. Helping appears to be a default behavior that culture can enhance or suppress but does not create from scratch.
takeaways: Toddlers help strangers spontaneously before age two
Helping does not require explicit teaching or rewards
Rewards can actually reduce intrinsic prosocial motivation

faq.question: What kind of helping do toddlers show?
faq.answer: Toddlers pick up dropped objects for adults, open doors, point to indicate information, and share food. These behaviors emerge spontaneously around 14 to 18 months. Importantly, they help even when the adult has not asked, suggesting an intrinsic motivation to assist.

faq.question: Why might rewarding helping actually backfire?
faq.answer: Studies show that toddlers who receive material rewards for helping later help less than those who received no reward. Extrinsic rewards may undermine intrinsic motivation by turning a natural impulse into a transactional exchange, a phenomenon called the overjustification effect.
